paragraphs.heading: A path through spacetime
paragraphs.text: A world line is the path an object traces through spacetime, where each event is labelled by four numbers: one for time and three for position. Usually the object is treated as a point, like a particle or an observer, and its world line is the string of events that make up its history. Each point on the line is an event, marked by a time and by where the object was at that time. Hermann Minkowski pioneered the idea, and today the term turns up mostly in special and general relativity.

paragraphs.heading: Earth's helix
paragraphs.text: Earth's yearly orbit shows why time matters. In space alone the orbit is close to a circle: every year Earth comes back to the same spot relative to the Sun. But it gets there at a later time. So in spacetime its world line is a helix, a coil that never returns to the same point.

paragraphs.heading: Reading a spacetime diagram
paragraphs.text: On a spacetime diagram, a vertical line, with the space coordinate held constant, is a particle at rest or an observer standing still. A tilted line is a particle moving at a steady speed, and the more it leans away from vertical, the faster it goes. A flat horizontal segment, by contrast, can stand for a rod at one moment of coordinate time; it is not a world line in the proper sense.

paragraphs.heading: Stories told by lines
paragraphs.text: Where two separate world lines meet, the diagram shows a collision or an encounter. Two lines that begin at the same event and then go their own ways can show one particle decaying into two, or one particle giving off another. A photon's world line, the path of light, can join a particle's line to an observer's line, picturing light sent out by the particle and later seen by the observer.

paragraphs.heading: Proper time
paragraphs.text: In more exact terms, a curve counts as a particle's world line if its tangent, its direction at each point, is future timelike everywhere. Measuring along the line gives a quantity called proper time, usually written τ, and the length of the whole line is called the particle's proper time. Proper time is the usual way to mark positions along a world line. If the world line is a straight segment, the particle is said to be in free fall.

paragraphs.heading: Strings and tubes
paragraphs.text: A world line follows a single point. A one-dimensional object such as a string sweeps out a two-dimensional surface instead, called a world sheet. For an open string with loose ends the sheet is a strip, and for a closed loop it looks like a tube. An object with real volume, not shrunk to a point, traces a world tube.

paragraphs.heading: A word of caution
paragraphs.text: People sometimes call any curve in spacetime a world line, and this loose use causes confusion. Properly, the term means a curve that records the history through time of a particle, an observer or a small object.
